🧐 1 in 5 workers wouldn't quit even if paid 120% of their salary to stop

Julian Jacobs of Oxford and Google DeepMind surveyed 8,234 working-age adults in the UK, US, Denmark and India. He asked what guaranteed income would make them leave their job.

Most would leave if offered their current salary. One in five would stay even at 120%.

Pay is the main reason to work for just over a quarter of people. A third value the work itself, nearly a quarter come for the people around them, and 17% for the status. These motives look the same across incomes and in white- and blue-collar jobs.

His conclusion: a basic income may be necessary if AI takes jobs, but it may not replace what work gives people beyond money. More in DeepMind's essay on the research.

📚 A free course on making AI coding agents reliable has over 22,000 GitHub stars

Learn Harness Engineering teaches the setup around the model: instructions, tools, environment, memory and checks that keep an agent like Claude Code or Codex on track. It has 14 lectures and 8 hands-on projects, in 15 languages, under the MIT license.

Highlights from the latest updates:
1. Build a loop where one agent does the work and another checks it, instead of prompting by hand.
2. Grow the loop into a graph with parallel steps, a rollback path and a human approval step.
3. Breakdowns of how Claude Code, Codex, DeepSeek and Pi build their own harnesses.
4. A ready skill that sets up AGENTS.md, feature lists and verification steps for your project.

It builds on OpenAI's and Anthropic's engineering posts on harness design. The course is on GitHub.

👽 AI agents now run the telescope that listens for aliens

At the Allen Telescope Array in Northern California, scientists can type one plain-English request and AI agents handle the rest: they steer the antennas, calibrate and focus the instrument, catch and fix data errors and plot the result.

The SETI Institute and Breakthrough Listen built it with Nvidia, which announced it on October 30. Up to 2.4 terabits of data per second flow straight into GPUs next to the dishes, so signals are processed on the fly instead of piling up on hard drives.

Nvidia says the agents squeeze weeks or years of human work into hours. The pipeline has already made the first real-time AI detection of a pulsar, a spinning dead star that blinks like a lighthouse, in the Crab Nebula.

Next, the team is testing open models for observatories that may someday run offline on the far side of the Moon.

😐 OpenAI wants you to stop calling them data centers

The new name is "AI compute campuses." OpenAI will start pushing it right after Tuesday's midterms, as towns across the US push back against new data centers, Axios reports.

The rebrand is part of a policy blitz that starts when Congress returns on Nov 9:
• mandatory "speed limits" for the most powerful AI, so humans keep their hands on the wheel
• deals with host towns, plus state bills that give locals a say in how projects are built and what they get back
• training and support for workers hit by AI
• a push for the US to set global AI standards

Axios expects a harsher Washington for AI companies, with Democrats likely to win the House. OpenAI's global affairs chief Chris Lehane is already looking further ahead:

"AI is going to be the issue in 2028."

🧐 A model 660 times smaller beat 72B AIs at seeing the world like image models

Yann LeCun and Randall Balestriero say the way chatbots learn, by predicting the next word, is "a remarkably inefficient route" to a shared picture of the world.

AI models trained on text, images or sound may end up with the same inner picture of reality as they grow. Until now that was a guess. The new paper proves when it happens: the model must learn from two views of one scene, like a photo and its caption. Next-word prediction learns from pieces of the same document instead.

On the same texts, their method got as close to image models after 21.6 million training samples as next-word prediction did after 900 million. A 109-million-parameter text model also lined up with image AIs better than every language model they tested, up to Qwen2.5-72B.

The paper, from LeCun's AMI Labs, NYU and Brown, came out on October 29.

💰 An African developer recreated a $1.3 million startup idea in just 9 minutes

On October 30, YC-backed startup Subvocal announced a $1.3 million funding round led by Y Combinator and Afore Capital.

Its product? Smart glasses that convert silent speech into text by detecting tiny movements in facial muscles. According to the company, the technology can process more than 200 words per minute.

But just one day later, developer Joe Blau demonstrated a surprisingly different approach.

He built an experimental application for AirPods Pro 3 that attempts to detect silent speech using the headphones’ built-in accelerometer and gyroscope.

The idea is simple, even when you don’t speak aloud, silently forming words creates tiny movements that can be detected through sensors. His software reportedly reads these signals around 25 times per second.

Blau claims he built the application in just 9 minutes using AI-assisted coding, commonly known as vibecoding.

A $1.3 million startup versus a developer with AirPods and 9 minutes of coding.

Of course, a quick prototype is not necessarily a replacement for Subvocal’s dedicated hardware or a proven product. But it’s another example of how AI-assisted development is lowering the barrier to building experimental technology.
